newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cbank says raises one-yr credit to $2.0 bln.
newsitem.headline: Czech cbank says raises one-yr credit to $2.0 bln.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) said on Monday it had raised the amount of its one-year revolving credit facility arranged by four international banks to $2.0 billion from $1.5 billion due to high syndicate demand.

"The facility will be for $2.0 billion and this is because of the large interest of banks to participate in this," CNB spokesman Martin Svehla told Reuters. "But all of the conditions for the credit facility remain the same."

The credit is priced at 10 basis points above Libor, but with stipulations. According to Svehla, the facility has a fee of five basis points above Libor "plus the margin of five basis points, so 10 (basis points) together".
The facility at that rate would represent the cheapest credit granted to a post-Communist borrower.

Svehla has said there are also conditions which would trigger a utilisation fee connected to the volume of credit actually drawn, but he referred further comment on the conditions to syndicate members.
Svehla did not comment further on the credit.
On May 6, the CNB mandated Chase Investment Bank Ltd, Commerzbank AG, JP Morgan Securities Ltd and SBC Warburg, a division of Swiss Bank Corp, to arrange the credit.
The Financial Times has reported that an additional 2.5 basis points would be added to the rate if more than 50 percent of the facility is drawn.
The credit is to be placed with a limited group of core relationship banks, and is to act as a standby to strengthen the CNB's foreign exchange reserves, the CNB has said.
The credit is priced below the Czech Export Bank's recently concluded $250 million Eurobond which came in at 12.5 basis points above the London Interbank Offered Rate (Libor).

CNB reserves were just over $11 billion at the end of April, before several CNB currency market interventions in late May -- which analysts estimated at between $1 billion and $3 billion -- to bolster the Czech crown against speculative attacks.

The Czech Republic carries investment-grade sovereign debt ratings of "A" from Standard & Poor's and BAA1 from Moody's. S&P officials said on May 23 that they were keeping the Czech rating steady despite the pressure on the crown.

The crown had lost more than 15 percent of its value against major currencies since February, but strengthened in recent days as the government launched its austerity programme and narrowly won a parliamentary vote of confidence.

The Czech Republic paid off its entire $471 million in post-Communist transformation credit granted by the IMF ahead of schedule in 1994, because of strong growth in foreign exchange reserves. The debt was scheduled to be paid off between 1996 and 1999.
Foreign reserves grew backed by a fixed exchange rate and strong interest yield differentials against major currencies.
